title: DHCP Enterprise Troubleshooting
subject: DHCP
description: Practice troubleshooting common DHCP problems using evidence-first triage, diagnosis, and fix decisions. Titles and summaries are symptom-based so the workflow reveals the root cause.
reportOverview: This report summarizes your ticket outcomes and change notes for DHCP concepts practice. Use it to reinforce what evidence led you to each decision.
evidenceInstructions:
Instructions:
1) Read the observed symptom and scan the evidence.
2) Decide what you should verify first (Triage).
3) Choose the most likely cause based on the evidence (Diagnosis).
4) Select the best remediation action (Fix).
5) Write a short change note describing what changed and how you validated it.

tickets.title: New DHCP server shows running but clients cannot obtain leases
tickets.summary: A newly installed DHCP server shows the service as running, but the DHCP console shows a red down arrow and clients cannot obtain IP addresses from it.
artifact: "The DHCP service is not authorized to start."
validations: Confirm DHCP server is authorized in AD.
Confirm console icon turns normal and leases issue.
Renew a client lease successfully.
tickets.debrief: In a Windows Domain environment, DHCP servers must be 'Authorized' in Active Directory before they will respond to client requests. This is a security feature designed to prevent unauthorized (rogue) servers from disrupting the network. Even if the 'DHCP Server' service status is 'Running' in services.msc, the application-level logic will remain dormant until it verifies its authorized status in the AD configuration container.

triage.q: What should you verify FIRST on the new DHCP server node?
options: The status of the DHCP Server service in services.msc
Whether the server has been authorized within Active Directory
If the IPv4 Scope has been activated
The Binding settings for the server's network interface

diagnosis.q: What is the MOST likely cause given Event ID 1046?
options: The DHCP service is disabled by Group Policy
The scope has not been activated yet
The server is part of a domain but lacks AD authorization
There is a rogue DHCP server preventing this one from starting

fix.q: Which action is the best fix?
options: Right-click the server in the DHCP console and select 'Authorize'
Restart the Domain Controller to refresh AD permissions
Reinstall the DHCP Server Role via Server Manager
Manually start the DHCP Server service from the command line

tickets.title: Internal resources unreachable by name after lease renewal
tickets.summary: A new batch of computers can ping internal servers by IP address, but they cannot resolve internal names or complete domain-related tasks.
validations: Confirm clients receive DNS server IPs via DHCP.
Confirm nslookup resolves internal names.
Confirm domain operations proceed normally.
tickets.debrief: A successful DHCP 'DORA' process provides more than just an IP; it delivers the 'Scope Options' necessary for network participation. Option 006 (DNS Servers) is critical in Active Directory environments because clients use it to find Domain Controllers. Without it, the DNS field remains blank, and name resolution defaults to external or broadcast methods which fail for internal resources.

triage.q: Which section of the DHCP console should be examined to investigate missing client settings?
options: Server Options or Scope Options
Address Leases
The Exclusion list within the Scope
DHCP Policies and Filters

diagnosis.q: What is the MOST likely cause of the blank DNS field on the client?
options: The DNS Server service is down on the DC
Option 006 (DNS Servers) is not configured in the DHCP scope
The client is not a member of the DnsUpdateProxy group
The DHCP server cannot reach the DNS server to register records

fix.q: Which action is the best fix?
options: Add a static DNS entry in the client's host file
Enable 'Always dynamically update DNS records' in Scope properties
Configure Scope Option 006 with the IPs of the internal DNS servers
Configure Scope Option 015 with the DNS Domain Name

tickets.title: Intermittent 'Limited Connectivity' as the office fills up
tickets.summary: Early arrivals have working connectivity, but later arrivals cannot get online and show limited connectivity on their devices.
artifact: Client IP becomes 169.254.x.x (APIPA) after renew attempts
validations: Confirm address availability increases after remediation.
Renew on multiple clients succeeds.
Monitor scope utilization stays below capacity.
tickets.debrief: Scope exhaustion is a common issue in high-density environments like modern offices. When the available pool hits zero, the server simply ignores DHCP Discover packets. This forces clients to self-assign an APIPA address (169.254.x.x). To fix this, you must either expand the address range or shorten the lease duration to reclaim IPs from 'stale' devices (like users who leave the office) more quickly.

triage.q: What should you check FIRST to investigate the lack of available IPs?
options: The list of Address Leases and the Scope Statistics
The DHCP Audit logs for 'DENIED' messages
The Failover tab to see if the partner server is down
The 'Allow' filter list for missing MAC addresses

diagnosis.q: What is the MOST likely cause of 100% utilization?
options: The lease duration is too short, causing constant renewals
The scope range is too small for the current number of active devices
The DHCP database is corrupted and showing incorrect stats
A malicious user is performing a DNS poisoning attack

fix.q: Which action is the best fix for long-term capacity management?
options: Delete all current leases to clear the database
Disable the scope and recreate it with a larger range
Extend the address range in Scope Properties and shorten the lease duration
Switch the failover mode from Load Balance to Hot Standby

tickets.title: Connectivity lost only when switching to wired dock
tickets.summary: A laptop receives a valid IP address on Wi-Fi, but when connected via a docking station it fails to obtain an IP address.
artifact: An Allow filter is enabled on the DHCP server.
Wi-Fi MAC is present in Allow list; dock MAC is not.
validations: Confirm dock MAC is included where needed.
Renew succeeds while docked.
Confirm correct scope/options are applied.
tickets.debrief: DHCP Link Layer filtering (MAC filtering) is an effective but high-maintenance security control. Because a laptop uses a different MAC address for its Wi-Fi card than it does for its docking station (or built-in Ethernet), you must ensure every potential NIC is authorized. If 'Allow' filters are enabled, the server will drop requests from any MAC not explicitly listed, leading to a timeout on the client.

triage.q: Given that Wi-Fi works but the dock fails, what should you verify on the DHCP server?
options: If there is a conflict between the Wi-Fi and Docking station IP reservations
The status of DHCP Server Filters (Allow/Deny lists)
If the Ethernet VLAN has a different Scope Option 003
If the DHCP Failover partner is synchronized

diagnosis.q: What is the MOST likely cause of the timeout while docked?
options: The dock's MAC address is not permitted by the 'Allow' filter
The dock's NIC does not support DHCP Option 81
The scope for the wired network is currently exhausted
The dock is being identified as a Rogue DHCP server

fix.q: Which action is the best fix?
options: Disable the Wi-Fi card whenever the laptop is docked
Add the Docking Station's MAC address to the 'Allow' filter
Create an exclusion for the laptop's current Wi-Fi IP
Increase the Maximum Client Lead Time (MCLT) in failover

tickets.title: Workstation pulling IP from unknown range
tickets.summary: A user’s computer shows it is connected, but it receives an IP address that does not match the organization’s addressing and cannot access internal resources.
validations: Confirm authorized DHCP servers are the only responders.
Renew results in an organizational IP range.
Consider preventive controls (e.g., switch protections) where appropriate.
tickets.debrief: Rogue DHCP servers—often a consumer router plugged in by an employee—respond to client 'Discover' packets faster than the enterprise server. The first server to respond with an 'Offer' usually wins the lease. By checking 'ipconfig /all', you can see the 'DHCP Server' IP; if it doesn't match your server list, you have a rogue device. Modern networks use 'DHCP Snooping' on switches to block unauthorized DHCP traffic at the port level.

triage.q: What is the first step in identifying the source of the 192.168.1.1 address?
options: Check the DHCP Server's 'Address Leases' for the 192.168 range
Run a packet capture or use 'ping -a' to identify the device at 192.168.1.1
Check if the server's second NIC is accidentally configured with that IP
Verify if a Superscope was recently created on the DC

diagnosis.q: What is the MOST likely cause of this behavior?
options: The internal DHCP server has a secondary IP bound to its interface
A rogue DHCP server or unauthorized router is present on the network segment
The user has manually configured an Alternate Configuration in IPv4 properties
The DHCP Relay Agent is pointing to the wrong IP address

fix.q: Which action is the best fix?
options: Create a new Scope on the DC that matches the 192.168.1.0/24 range
Enable DHCP Snooping on the network switches and remove the rogue device
Authorize the 192.168.1.1 server in Active Directory
Configure the client to use a static IP to bypass the rogue server

tickets.title: Address flagged as 'BAD_ADDRESS' in console
tickets.summary: A specific IP address keeps being marked as unusable in the DHCP console, and clients sometimes report IP conflicts.
artifact: A printer is configured manually with a static IP address.
validations: Confirm the static device IP is excluded from the DHCP pool.
Remove conflict entry if appropriate and observe it does not return.
Verify clients no longer report IP conflict warnings.
tickets.debrief: The 'BAD_ADDRESS' flag is the result of the DHCP server's 'Conflict Detection' logic. Before issuing an IP, the server pings it; if it gets a reply, it knows a device (like a manually configured printer) is already using that address. It marks the address as BAD to prevent duplicate assignments. The correct fix is to 'Exclude' that IP from the dynamic range so the server never tries to assign it to begin with.

triage.q: What does a 'BAD_ADDRESS' entry typically indicate in a Windows DHCP console?
options: The DHCP database has a corrupted record for that IP
The DHCP server detected the IP was already in use via conflict detection (ping)
The IP address is reserved for a MAC that no longer exists
The client failed to register its name in DNS for that IP

diagnosis.q: Why did the conflict occur with the printer?
options: The printer is using a MAC address that is already reserved
The printer's static IP (10.0.0.25) is part of the dynamic pool and wasn't excluded
The DHCP server's Conflict Detection Attempts is set to 0
The printer is acting as a secondary DHCP server

fix.q: Which action is the best fix?
options: Delete the BAD_ADDRESS entry and hope it doesn't return
Add 10.0.0.25 to the 'Exclusions' in the DHCP scope
Create a Reservation for the printer using its MAC address
Change the printer to obtain an IP automatically via DHCP

tickets.title: DHCP works on Floor 1 but fails for Floor 2
tickets.summary: Clients on one floor (separate VLAN/subnet) cannot obtain DHCP addresses, while clients on the same VLAN as the server work normally.
artifact: Clients on Floor-2 VLAN get 169.254.x.x after renew attempts.
Clients on Floor-1 VLAN obtain leases normally.
No requests appear from the Floor-2 subnet in DHCP logs.
validations: Confirm DHCP relay/helper is configured for the VLAN interface.
Confirm DORA exchange completes for Floor-2 clients.
Renew succeeds on Floor-2 clients.
tickets.debrief: DHCP discovery relies on Layer 2 broadcasts, which routers do not forward by default. To serve clients on a different VLAN, you must configure a 'DHCP Relay Agent' (often called an 'IP Helper' in Cisco terminology) on the gateway for that VLAN. This agent catches the broadcast and forwards it as a unicast packet to the DHCP server. If the server sees zero requests from a subnet, the issue is almost always the relay configuration.

triage.q: What should you verify FIRST regarding the network infrastructure between floors?
options: The presence of an IP Helper/DHCP Relay address on the Floor 2 gateway
If the Floor 2 scope has been authorized in Active Directory
If the DHCP server has a secondary NIC for the Floor 2 VLAN
The 'Server Options' in the DHCP console

diagnosis.q: What is the MOST likely reason the server sees no requests from Floor 2?
options: The Floor 2 subnet is too large for the DHCP server to process
DHCP broadcast packets are being blocked by the router/Layer-3 switch
The Floor 2 clients are using IPv6 and ignoring the DHCPv4 server
The DHCP service is only bound to the Floor 1 IP address

fix.q: Which action is the best fix?
options: Create a new Scope for Floor 2 and activate it
Install a second DHCP server on the Floor 2 VLAN
Configure the router interface for Floor 2 with the 'ip helper-address' of the DHCP server
Enable 'Broadcast' flag on all Floor 2 workstations

tickets.title: Redundancy fails: Secondary server not issuing leases
tickets.summary: One DHCP server is down, but clients are not obtaining leases from the second server as expected. The failover status shows an error state.
artifact: DHCP failover status on partner server:
When DHCP1 is stopped, new clients fail to obtain leases.
validations: Confirm failover relationship shows healthy/normal state.
Confirm leases issue while one partner is down.
Confirm lease replication behaves normally.
tickets.debrief: DHCP Failover (introduced in Server 2012) requires continuous synchronization between partners. 'Communication Interrupted' means the partners can't hear each other, but they haven't reached the 'Partner Down' state yet. Crucially, if the secondary server was never fully synchronized, it doesn't have a copy of the scopes to issue. Keeping failover healthy requires the same shared secret and TCP port 647 to be open between servers.

triage.q: What does 'Communication Interrupted' status typically suggest?
options: The secondary server's DHCP service has crashed
The two servers cannot talk to each other over the failover port (647)
The Active Directory domain is unreachable by both servers
The DHCP database has reached its maximum size limit

diagnosis.q: Why would clients fail to get an IP from the partner during an outage?
options: The standby server only has 5% of the IP pool available
The failover synchronization failed, so the partner has no record of the scope
The Hot Standby server is waiting for the MCLT (Maximum Client Lead Time) to expire
The shared secret is incorrect, causing authentication to fail between servers

fix.q: Which action is the best fix?
options: Manually copy the DHCP database from Server 1 to Server 2
Replicate the scope manually by right-clicking and selecting 'Replicate Scope'
Delete and recreate the failover relationship, ensuring the shared secret and ports are open
Change the failover mode from 'Hot Standby' to 'Load Balance'

tickets.title: Updated reservation not taking effect
tickets.summary: An administrator changed a reservation to a new IP, but the client continues to use the previous IP address.
artifact: - Address Leases show an active lease for 10.0.0.50 for the same MAC
validations: Confirm the old lease is released/cleared as appropriate.
Renew results in the reserved address.
Confirm no duplicate reservation/lease remains.
tickets.debrief: A DHCP Reservation is a 'promise' of a specific IP for a specific MAC, but it doesn't override an existing lease instantly. DHCP is a pull-based system; the client only checks for updates at the T1 (renewal) interval—usually 50% of the lease time. To force a change, you must manually trigger an 'ipconfig /renew' on the client or delete the active lease record in the DHCP console to force the client to negotiate a new one.

triage.q: Why does the client still have 10.0.0.50 after the server change?
options: The DHCP server hasn't committed the database change to disk
The client has not yet reached its renewal interval (T1) to ask for a new lease
The reservation was made for the wrong MAC address
The client's static IP configuration is overriding the DHCP reservation

diagnosis.q: What is preventing the client from picking up the .60 address immediately?
options: The DHCP server requires a restart to apply reservations
The client still has a valid, unexpired lease for the old IP address
Reservations can only be applied to devices that are currently offline
The client is getting a response from a secondary DHCP server instead

fix.q: Which action is the best fix?
options: Delete the client's host record in DNS
Run 'ipconfig /release' and 'ipconfig /renew' on the client machine
Change the Reservation IP back to .50 and then to .60 again
Reboot the DHCP server to force all clients to reconnect

tickets.title: Limited communication after scope reconfiguration
tickets.summary: Clients receive an IP address but cannot communicate outside their immediate subnet segment. Only a small group of hosts are reachable.
artifact: Servers reside on 10.0.0.0/16 and should be reachable from this segment.
validations: Confirm clients receive correct mask after remediation.
Confirm clients can reach intended subnets.
Confirm scope configuration matches network design.
tickets.debrief: The Subnet Mask defines the 'local' boundaries of a network. If the mask is too restrictive (e.g., /24 instead of /16), the client thinks IPs that are actually on its local segment are on a different network. It then tries to send that traffic to the Default Gateway. If the router isn't prepared to handle that specific traffic flow, communication fails. Note: In Windows DHCP, the subnet mask is defined at scope creation and cannot be edited; you must recreate the scope to change it.

triage.q: Comparing the client IP and Mask to the Network Design note, what stands out?
options: The Default Gateway is in the wrong subnet
The Subnet Mask (255.255.255.0) is more restrictive than the design (10.0.0.0/16)
The IP address is outside the 10.0.0.0 range
The DHCP server is not providing a DNS suffix

diagnosis.q: What is the MOST likely cause of the communication failure?
options: The router is blocking traffic between 10.0.30.x and 10.0.0.x
The incorrect subnet mask causes the client to believe 10.0.0.x is on a different network requiring a gateway
The client has the wrong DNS server configured in DHCP Option 006
The DHCP scope has run out of /16 addresses

fix.q: Which action is the best fix?
options: Change the Subnet Mask in the existing Scope properties
Manually set the subnet mask on every workstation to 255.255.0.0
Delete and recreate the DHCP scope with the correct /16 (255.255.0.0) subnet mask
Add a static route to the client's routing table
